name: Oracle
summary: Oracle hires engineers across its database, cloud infrastructure and enterprise applications businesses, and candidates commonly report interviews built on computer science fundamentals, databases and SQL, and a close look at their own projects. For campus and early-career roles, many describe an online test followed by technical interviews and an HR round; experienced roles usually add design and hiring manager conversations.
rounds: Online application and a recruiter or HR screen
Online test for many campus and early-career roles: aptitude, coding and computer science basics
One or two technical interviews: data structures, databases and SQL, operating systems, and your projects
Hiring manager interview on past work, design and how you'd fit the team
looks_for: Strong fundamentals: data structures, algorithms, operating systems and networks
Database knowledge: SQL, indexing, transactions and query performance
Cloud and distributed-systems thinking for cloud infrastructure roles
Clear explanations of your own projects and the decisions behind them
Care for enterprise customers: reliability, security and compatibility
Willingness to learn large, mature codebases

questions.text: Tell me about a time you had to understand a large, unfamiliar codebase quickly.
covers: What you needed to change and how little time you had
How you found your way: tracing a request, reading tests, asking the right people
What you delivered and what you'd do faster next time

questions.text: Tell me about a time you handled a problem that was affecting a customer in production.
covers: The impact on the customer and how urgent it was
How you found the cause and kept people informed
The fix, and what stopped it happening again

questions.text: Tell me about a time you disagreed with a more senior colleague on a technical approach.
covers: Both approaches, described fairly
How you made your case with evidence
The decision and how you supported it

questions.text: Tell me about the project that taught you the most, including what went wrong.
covers: What the project was and your role in it
What went wrong and your share of it
The lesson and where you've used it since

questions.text: Explain what happens inside a database when you run a query with a join and a filter.
covers: Parsing, then the optimiser choosing a plan
Using indexes for the filter, and join methods such as nested loops, hash or merge joins
How to read an execution plan to see what it actually did

questions.text: What are transactions and isolation levels, and which problems do they prevent?
covers: ACID in plain words
Problems such as dirty reads, non-repeatable reads and phantom rows
The trade-off between stricter isolation and concurrency

questions.text: When would you add an index to a table, and when could an index make things worse?
covers: Columns used in frequent filters, joins and sorting
The cost: slower writes, more storage, and indexes the optimiser ignores
Checking the effect with the query plan and real workloads

questions.text: How would you design a multi-tenant cloud service so one customer's heavy use doesn't slow down others?
covers: Isolation options: separate resources, shared resources with quotas, or a mix
Rate limits, fair scheduling and monitoring per tenant
What happens when a tenant hits its limit, and how you'd communicate it

questions.text: Explain the difference between virtual machines and containers, and when you'd choose each.
covers: A VM runs a full operating system; containers share the host's kernel
Trade-offs in isolation, start-up time and density
Examples where each fits, such as strong isolation versus many small services

questions.text: A customer's nightly batch job now takes twice as long as it used to. How would you investigate?
covers: What changed: data volume, code, configuration, or other jobs running at the same time
Comparing execution plans and resource use with an earlier run
A fix for tonight and a lasting fix

questions.text: How would you design a service that backs up customer databases and restores them to any point in time?
covers: Full backups plus continuous log capture, replayed to the chosen moment
Storage tiers, retention and encryption
Testing restores regularly, since an untested backup can't be trusted

questions.text: Explain how garbage collection works in Java, and how you'd spot a memory leak in a Java service.
covers: Reachability, generations, and why most objects die young
How a leak still happens: references kept in caches, listeners or static collections
Finding it with heap dumps, GC logs and memory trends over time

questions.text: Tell me about yourself and the project you'd most like to discuss today.
covers: A short path: your studies or work so far and what you focus on now
One project, the problem it solved and your part in it
Why that leads you to this role

questions.text: Why Oracle, and which part of its business (database, cloud or applications) interests you most?
covers: A specific area and what you know about it
A link to your skills, coursework or projects
What you want to learn there

tips: Revise SQL and database internals thoroughly; joins, indexes, transactions and query plans come up often for Oracle roles.
If your role uses Java, know collections, garbage collection and concurrency well; Oracle develops the Java platform.
For cloud infrastructure roles, practise designing for failure: replication, fault isolation, quotas and safe rollouts.
Be ready to explain every line of your résumé; technical interviews commonly start from your projects.
For campus roles, practise aptitude and coding questions under time limits before the online test.
